judgments.reasoning_cat1: The parenthetical "(“EGL” or the “Guarantor” as the case may be)" leaves it unclear when each label operates, and the preamble makes the Borrower a party to an instrument the cover page describes as "made by ESSAR GLOBAL LIMITED in favor of ICICI". Beyond that the recitation of parties is conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Borrower's status as a party matters because Section 2.02(d)/(f) and Article III(o) impose obligations on the Borrower while Article III's introduction is framed as the Guarantor's representations, and Section 4.15 limits third-party rights to "the Lenders" though the Facility Agent and Borrower are parties. That mismatch is a real, if modest, whole-instrument tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A plain recital that the Lenders have severally agreed to extend credit on the Credit Agreement's terms; nothing vague or grammatically defective. No catch-all list.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with Section 2.01 and the definition of Borrower Obligations, both of which assume extensions of credit under the Credit Agreement. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Affiliated group of companies" is loose but the recital states a bare fact and imposes no obligation. Little for a court to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supports the benefit recital and the guarantee itself; no operative provision turns on group membership. Nothing contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Substantial direct and indirect benefit" is a conclusory, unquantified phrase that becomes contestable in a solvency or reasonably-equivalent-value fight. Otherwise the recital is unremarkable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits alongside the solvency representation in Article III(e) and the fraudulent-conveyance cap in Section 2.01(b)(ii), which contemplate that the guarantee could exceed what EGL can lawfully guarantee — a recital-versus-operative tension worth noting but not a squarely opposed term.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard condition-precedent recital identifying the guarantee as an inducement; the terms are definite. Nothing ambiguous to name.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the consideration clause and Section 2.01; the "ratable benefit of the Lenders" phrase recurs consistently. No conflicting provision located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Boilerplate consideration language, definite in its terms. No named ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the recitals and with the operative guarantee in Section 2.01; "ratable benefit" is used throughout. Nothing to reconcile.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Unless the context requires otherwise" is an escape hatch, but this is the ordinary incorporation-of-defined-terms formula. Low intrinsic risk.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It makes the Credit Agreement's definitions govern undefined capitalized terms, which is how "Commercial Operations Date", "Required Lenders" and "Project" work here; it does sit against Section 1.03's declaration that this Agreement controls over other Loan Documents. That tension is mild since 1.03 is limited to matters covered hereby.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A self-referential definition with a standard amendment tail; nothing uncertain. No list or catch-all issue.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Used consistently throughout; no amendment mechanism in the Agreement conflicts with it. No issue found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition piles "including", "all other obligations and liabilities" and "or otherwise" onto enumerated items, leaving the outer reach of the guaranteed debt contestable, and the text is interrupted by stray running-header words ("if EGL Guarantee Agreement any"). The general-after-specific structure is the classic 1.3 pattern.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on "Obligations (as defined in the Credit Agreement)" while Section 1.01's own "Obligations" definition points back to Borrower Obligations — a circularity; and its breadth must be squared with the $250,000,000 cap in Section 2.01(a)(iii) and the cap in 2.01(b)(ii). Those relationships give a court something to work with.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Any actual shortfall, howsoever caused, in funds available to the Borrower required" is grammatically broken against clause (ii) ("required: ... (ii) any increase in the cost"), and clause (ii) largely repeats clause (i), so the boundary of a Deficiency is genuinely uncertain; "as determined by the Borrower or the Required Lenders" leaves two potentially conflicting determinations. These are nameable defects.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The definition drives the funding obligation in Section 2.01(a)(ii) and the notice machinery in Section 2.02(a)–(b), which assume a single ascertainable amount certified by the Lender's Engineering Consultant; if Borrower and Required Lenders determine different amounts the Agreement gives no tie-breaker. That is a live incoherence.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single sentence of several hundred words in which the operative verb ("becomes effective") is stranded far from its subject, and the release turns on offtake agreements "reasonably acceptable" in "form and substance and for a term" — a discretionary standard whose boundary is contestable. The good-faith negotiation proviso adds a further indefinite obligation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This date is the primary termination trigger in Section 2.01(d) and bounds clause (iii) of Section 2.01(a), so any uncertainty about when it occurs propagates to the life of the guarantee; it also has to be squared with Section 2.06 reinstatement and Section 2.03's "paid in full in cash" condition. The interlock is real though not squarely contradictory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A pure cross-reference to Section 2.01(a); nothing ambiguous on its own face. Risk depends entirely on the referenced text.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.01(a) lumps three structurally different undertakings — including the Deficiency funding owed to the Borrower — into "Guarantor Obligations", yet Sections 2.03, 2.05 and 2.07 speak of Guarantor Obligations being paid to the Lenders in cash. That mismatch is imported wholesale by this definition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Material adverse effect" on "business, financial condition, operations or performance or properties ... since the date of this Agreement" is an inherently open-textured standard, and the doubled "or performance or properties" reads as a drafting slip. Materiality definitions are frequently the named ambiguity in disputes.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The term qualifies Article III(a), (c), (d) and the notice covenant in (m), and is used consistently; no provision contradicts it. The risk is intrinsic rather than relational.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition is a two-line pointer with no independent content, but it defines "Obligations" by reference to "Borrower Obligations", which is itself defined by reference to "the Obligations (as defined in the Credit Agreement)". That circularity is visible on the face of the pair.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 4.02(c) makes the indemnities survive "repayment of the Obligations", so which body of debt is meant — the Borrower's, the Guarantor's, or the Credit Agreement's — depends on resolving the circle. That is a genuine whole-instrument wrinkle.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Clause (e) expressly abolishes ejusdem generis ("a general statement ... shall not be limited to matters similar to the matters specifically mentioned"), which is itself the general-versus-specific battleground and would be argued over wherever a catch-all appears. The remaining rules are standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The rule bears directly on the open-ended lists in the Borrower Obligations definition and in Sections 2.04 and 2.05, expanding rather than contradicting them. No opposing provision found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "For the purposes of and to the extent of the matters covered by this Agreement" is a self-limiting qualifier whose scope is not obvious, but the priority rule itself is clear. Moderate intrinsic risk.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It declares this Agreement supreme over other Loan Documents, yet Section 1.01 takes its definitions from the Credit Agreement, Section 2.02(d) subjects Promoter Loans to "the provisions and requirements of the Credit Agreement", and Section 2.03 defers to Credit Agreement Section 6.07. Which instrument controls in those pockets is a real question.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The three clauses divide the guarantee into periods that do not obviously abut — clause (i) runs to satisfaction of Credit Agreement conditions, clause (ii) to the Commercial Operations Date, clause (iii) from that date — leaving uncertain whether a full payment guarantee exists in the interval; and the $250,000,000 proviso is expressly tied only to "this clause (iii)", inviting argument about whether the earlier clauses are uncapped. Clause (ii)'s obligation runs to the Borrower, not the Lenders, yet is folded into the same defined term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be reconciled with Section 2.01(b)(ii)'s separate fraudulent-conveyance cap, with Section 2.01(d)'s termination on the earlier of the Release Date or payment in full, and with Section 2.02's notice machinery on which clause (ii) is conditioned while 2.02(b) says no one need give notice. Those interlocks are exactly where a construction fight would arise.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Clause (i) is ungrammatical — "the obligations of the Guarantor hereunder are primary and notwithstanding the obligations of any other Person" is missing words and does not parse as written, so what it does to the primacy of the guarantee is uncertain. That is a nameable mechanical defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its "anything herein ... to the contrary notwithstanding" cap sits alongside the separate $250,000,000 cap in Section 2.01(a)(iii), and the two limits are not related to each other. A court would have to decide how they interact.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, definite acknowledgment that the guaranteed debt may exceed the guarantor's capped liability. Nothing vague.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It presupposes the caps in Sections 2.01(a)(iii) and 2.01(b)(ii) and is consistent with them. No conflict located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Until the earlier of" is clear, though clause (ii) stacks three conditions (payment in full, no Letter of Credit outstanding, Commitments terminated) that read as cumulative. Little intrinsic ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Termination on the "earlier" of the EGL Guarantee Release Date can release the guarantee while Borrower Obligations remain unpaid, which is hard to square with Section 2.05's "absolute and unconditional" guarantee, with Section 2.03's subrogation bar keyed to payment in full, and with Section 2.06 reinstatement. It also does not address the Deficiency obligation, which Section 2.01(a)(ii) runs to the Commercial Operations Date.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The first sentence is garbled — "shall notify the Guarantor ... to the extent a Deficiency at any time exists and that the Guarantor provides to the Borrower the amount" omits the demand language and leaves the notice's required content unclear; likewise "may give a notice ... that the Guarantor provide". Whether the Engineering Consultant certification attaches to both routes of notice is also uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.01(a)(ii) conditions the Guarantor's funding duty on notice "as set forth in Section 2.02(a)", while Section 2.02(b) says neither Agent nor Lender need ever give notice — so the trigger can be withheld entirely, and the subsection lettering jumps (b) to (d) to (f). That combination is a genuine incoherence.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Neither the Facility Agent nor Lender" drops an article, and the exculpation for "demanding insufficient funds" is broad but its terms are plain. Modest intrinsic risk.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with Section 2.01(a)(ii) and 2.02(a), it means the Guarantor's Deficiency obligation may never be triggered, arguably hollowing out a principal undertaking of the Agreement; it also sits oddly against the Borrower's mandatory "shall notify" in 2.02(a). That is the kind of nullification argument courts entertain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It gives two funding routes without saying who chooses, then shifts to "If the Guarantor decides to contribute additional capital", implying the election is the Guarantor's; "charter capital" is an odd term for a Minnesota LLC. Those are nameable slips.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Lettered (d) with no (c) or (e) in the Agreement, and it makes the Promoter Loan route subject to the Credit Agreement notwithstanding Section 1.03's supremacy clause. Both are modest relational problems.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "To pay the cost or cost that has created the Deficiency" is a plain typographical duplication and the sentence structure leaves it unclear who pays. Minor but visible.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It repeats and partly overlaps Section 2.02(d) on the same subject and continues the broken (b)/(d)/(f) lettering, but does not contradict any other operative term. Low relational risk.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long but conventional subrogation waiver with a definite trigger ("until all Guarantor Obligations are paid in full in cash"). References to "any other Guarantor" are unexplained in a single-guarantor instrument.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The final carve-out defers to Section 6.07 of the Credit Agreement, which sits against Section 1.03's supremacy clause, and "any other Guarantor" points outside this instrument to the companion guarantee. Neither is a squarely opposed term.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The heading is "with respect to the Borrower Obligations" but the body repeatedly says "Guarantor Obligations" where amendments to the underlying debt are plainly meant, which changes what may be amended without discharging the guarantor. That is a nameable mechanical error.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 4.07 forbids using headings in construction, so the mismatch cannot be cured by the heading, and the reading affects Sections 2.01 and 2.05. The tension is real but secondary.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It uses "a Guaranteed Obligation", a capitalized term defined nowhere in this Agreement, and the closing definition of "demand" is unusual; otherwise the waivers are conventional and detailed. The stray undefined term is the identifiable defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: An "absolute and unconditional" guarantee "without regard to ... any other circumstance whatsoever" has to be reconciled with the express $250,000,000 cap in Section 2.01(a)(iii) and with the automatic release in Section 2.01(d). Courts routinely have to square those.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The reinstatement trigger is the insolvency or bankruptcy "of the Guarantor", where such clauses ordinarily key to the primary obligor whose payment is clawed back; the closing "or otherwise" is an unbounded catch-all after specifics. Both are visible on the face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Because the Borrower is the entity whose payments would be avoided, the clause may not operate as the guarantee structure in Section 2.01 and the termination rule in 2.01(d)(ii) assume. That is a plausible but not certain incoherence.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Guarantees that payments by it hereunder will be paid" is circular phrasing, but the substance — no set-off or counterclaim, in Dollars — is definite. Low risk.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It bars the Guarantor's set-off while Section 4.04 grants the Agent and Lenders wide set-off rights; the asymmetry is intentional, not contradictory. Section 2.01(a)(ii) contemplates payment to the Borrower rather than the Lenders, a slight mismatch with "paid to the Lenders".

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard bring-down formula; "each other date on which representations ... are made or deemed made under the Credit Agreement" is definite by reference. Nothing ambiguous to name.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The introduction frames everything that follows as representations and warranties, yet Article III(h), (l), (m), (n) and (o) are forward-looking covenants and (o) binds the Borrower, not the Guarantor — a mismatch the Article heading ("Representations, Warranties and Covenants") only partly cures given Section 4.07. That is a genuine relational defect.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Conventional corporate-status representation with a Material Adverse Effect qualifier on clause (iii). Nothing distinctive to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Material Adverse Effect definition and with the authority representation in (b). No conflict located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard authority and enforceability language with the usual bankruptcy and equitable-principles carve-outs; terms are definite. Low risk.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The absolute statement that no Governmental Authority consent or filing is required sits slightly against Article III(c)'s stamp-duty language and Section 4.02(b)'s stamp-tax indemnity, but not squarely. Nothing else conflicts.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Any other statutory duties and levies" is a catch-all following "stamp duty, registration charges", leaving its reach uncertain, though the rest is standard no-conflict language. Modest 1.3 exposure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The representation that no stamp duty is payable except what is already paid sits against Section 4.02(b), under which the Guarantor indemnifies for "any and all stamp, excise, sales or other taxes which may be payable" on this Agreement. The two can be harmonised but pull in different directions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Would ... reasonably be expect to result" is an obvious grammatical error, and "threatened" litigation is knowledge-qualified only in part. The error does not much change meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Material Adverse Effect definition and the notice covenant in (m). No conflicting provision found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional solvency representation; "unreasonably small capital" is a term of art from fraudulent-transfer law rather than a drafting vagueness. Low intrinsic risk.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is directly relevant to the fraudulent-conveyance ceiling in Section 2.01(b)(ii) and to the benefit recital, and the two are consistent rather than opposed. No conflict identified.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Shall at all time rank" is a typographical slip, and the clause mixes a present representation with a forward promise ("shall ... at all time") about "present and future senior Indebtedness". The pari passu formula "in right of payment in insolvency" is narrower than the usual wording, which invites argument.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing else in the Agreement addresses ranking or subordination of the Guarantor Obligations, so there is no provision to conflict with. Low relational risk.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "None of the or governors or managers" is plainly garbled, and "substantial Equity Interest" and "specified near relation" are boundary-less without external definition. The defects are visible but of little commercial consequence.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It refers to "Disclosed Matters", a term supplied only by the Credit Agreement, which is consistent with Section 1.01's incorporation. No conflict located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It blends a present representation with a continuing covenant ("this obligation shall be a covenant ... during the term of this Agreement") and refers to "the Facility", a term not defined here; "expeditious and effective steps" is an unmeasured standard. Several nameable soft spots.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cross-refers to Section 4.13 (Patriot Act), which is a notification provision rather than a requirement, so "in addition to the requirements of Section 4.13" is an imprecise fit; it also appears within an Article introduced as representations only. Modest relational risk.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The middle limb refers to immunity "attributed to the Borrower" in the midst of a Guarantor immunity waiver — apparently a carry-over error that changes whose immunity is waived. That is a clear mechanical defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Borrower is a party here, so the stray reference is not incoherent, but it does not match the Guarantor-only framing of the Article III introduction. Limited relational exposure.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "No Default in respect of the Guarantor" uses a Credit Agreement term built around the Borrower, so what a Guarantor-side Default is remains unstated. Short but genuinely open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 4.01 and Article III(m)(1) likewise assume Defaults can arise "in respect of" or be "known to" the Guarantor without the Agreement defining that concept. The gap is consistent across the instrument rather than contradictory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A carefully hedged information representation with an express carve-out for forward-looking material; the drafting is standard. "When taken as a whole" is soft but conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: "Confidential Information Material" is defined only in the Credit Agreement, which Section 1.01 permits. No conflicting provision found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Substantially more favorable to the beneficiary thereof" is an unmeasured comparative between whole guarantee packages, and "guarantee or other support" is an open catch-all; how one compares terms is not specified. A court would have a real question.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is a covenant lodged in an Article introduced as representations and warranties, and it presupposes other Project Lenders who are not Lenders here — a category the rest of the instrument does not develop. Modest relational tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The notice deadline and content are specific (five Business Days, Default or Material Adverse Effect). "Would reasonably be expected to" is standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is a covenant sitting inside the representations Article and depends on "Default" and "Responsible Officer" from the Credit Agreement; delivery "to the Lenders or the Facility Agent" is disjunctive where Section 4.12 sets a single notice regime. Minor friction only.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The closing proviso — that the restriction "shall not apply to an arms length sale or disposal of its assets or properties" — appears to swallow the prohibition it qualifies, since virtually any disposal could be characterised as arm's length; "materially and adversely affect the ability" is also unmeasured. The proviso-versus-covenant clash is nameable on the face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: If the proviso is read literally the Guarantor could dispose of everything and defeat the guarantee, which cannot be reconciled with the solvency representation in (e), the pari passu covenant in (f) or the purpose of Article II. That is precisely the nullification problem courts refuse to accept.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It speaks of "either Guarantor", "either Guarantee Agreement" and "the Parent" — none of which exist in an instrument with a single defined Guarantor and no defined Parent — and it binds the Borrower inside a Guarantor covenant. These are unmistakable carry-over errors.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 1.01 defines one "Guarantor" (EGL) and the preamble names only EGL and the Borrower, so "either Guarantor" and "the Parent" cannot be resolved within this instrument; the carve-out also defers to the Credit Agreement and the "Unrestricted Account", terms found only there. The provision cannot be applied without looking outside the four corners.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The carve-out "except by a written instrument pursuant to Section 4.12" points to the Notices provision, which contains no waiver or amendment mechanism, so the only route to an effective waiver is undefined. That is a mechanical cross-reference error that changes the clause's operation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Checked against Section 4.12 (Notices), Section 4.08 (Integration) and Section 4.14 (Entire Agreement): none of them supplies a written-waiver mechanism, and the Agreement contains no amendment clause at all. The mis-citation therefore is a defect in the provision's fit with the rest of the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Reasonable costs and expenses" and "reasonable fees and disbursements of counsel" are familiar, court-administrable standards. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Recovery of enforcement expenses is also folded into the Borrower Obligations definition, but the overlap is cumulative rather than contradictory. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Stamp, excise, sales or other taxes" is a general phrase after specifics, leaving the catch-all's reach (income or withholding taxes?) uncertain. That is a modest ejusdem generis point.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits against Article III(c)'s representation that no stamp duty or other statutory levy is payable except those already paid. The two coexist but pull against one another.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-sentence survival clause; "this Section" is unambiguous in context. Low risk.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It uses "the Obligations", a term whose Section 1.01 definition is circular, and survives past the release contemplated by Section 2.01(d). Minor only.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The prohibition and consent requirement are stated definitely; "binding upon the successors and assigns of the Guarantor" is standard. Nothing ambiguous to name.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 4.15 covers the identical ground but requires "the prior written consent of the Facility Agent and the Lenders", whereas this Section requires only the Facility Agent's consent — a direct inconsistency between two operative provisions of the same instrument. That is the clearest 2.1 candidate in the Agreement.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Long but precise: the trigger (continuing Event of Default), the property (deposits and other credits in any currency) and the obligations set off are all spelled out. Low intrinsic risk.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It refers to "any other Guarantor", who does not exist under this instrument, and its breadth complements rather than contradicts Section 2.07's bar on the Guarantor's own set-off. Modest relational exposure.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Ordinary counterparts clause; nothing uncertain. No list issue.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the two differing signature pages appended, and nothing else addresses execution formality except the "Executed as a Deed" legend. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard severability language with clear jurisdictional limits. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works alongside Section 2.01(b)(ii)'s statutory cap without contradiction. No issue found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clear instruction that headings do not affect construction. Nothing ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matters because Section 2.04's heading ("with respect to the Borrower Obligations") conflicts with its body's repeated "Guarantor Obligations"; this Section removes the heading as a cure. That gives it a small relational role rather than a defect of its own.
